newsitem.title: CHINA: Europe's AI(R) seeks to boost sales in China.
newsitem.headline: Europe's AI(R) seeks to boost sales in China.

text.p: European aircraft consortium Aero International Regional AI(R) plans to fly one of its ATR 72 turboprops around China as it seeks to build on an inital $100 million order there, the company said on Thursday.

AI(R) press and information director Giancarlo Fre Torelli said China's Xinjiang Airlines was due to take delivery of the country's first ATR 72-210A aircraft in the next couple of months. It is the first of five aircraft on firm order in a $100 million deal with another five on option.
Delivery will coincide with the sales demonstration tour to other interested Chinese airlines, Torelli said as he briefed journalists in Hong Kong on the company's Asian business strategy.

The AI(R) joint venture was in a strong position in Asia where the regional aircraft sector was forecast to grow at 13-15 percent in the near term, compared with a forecast for the rest of the world of 8-13 percent, Torelli added.
AI(R) is an French-Italian-British joint venture created by Aeropatiale, Alenia and British Aerospace for 40 to 110 seater turboprop and jet airliners.

Industry observers said the regional aircraft market in China is relatively undeveloped with Chinese airlines preferring larger jet aircraft. Torelli said the Chinese needed to review their priorities.
"The Chinese do need to reconsider their transportation philosophy in the short and long term to open up new routes and new connections," he said.
"We think in the long term, China is a good potential market for perhaps 10 aircraft per year," Torelli said.

AI(R) and Aviation Industries of China (AVIC) have signed a memorandum of understanding to study a joint venture to produce ATR 72 aircraft in China. Chinese companies already produce ATR fuselage parts.

AI(R) is also studying a new 58-70 seat twin engined regional jet, possibly with Asian help. A consortium of four Korean companies, Samsung, Daewoo, Hyundai and Korean Air, has agreed to initial participation in the project.
Taiwan Aerospace and a number of other companies, including Sweden's Saab Aircraft AB and Brazil's Embraer, are also potential risk sharing partners, Torelli said.
The new member of the AI(R) family would cost $1.2 billion to develop and viability studies are continuing.
